newsitem.title: UK: Eurostar float unscathed by tunnel fire fallout.
newsitem.headline: Eurostar float unscathed by tunnel fire fallout.

text.p: London and Continental Railways, owners of the Channel Tunnel passenger train service Eurostar, said on Thursday that a recent fire which swept through the tunnel would not derail its timetable for a flotation.

LCR chairman Sir Derek Hornby said the 1.0 billion pound ($1.6 billion) sale of Eurostar, which runs the express passenger trains between London, Paris and Brussels, was due within the next 18 months.
The group plans to outline details next summer, when it produces accounts for Eurostar for the year to December 31.

But Hornby conceded that since the November 18 fire -- which destroyed a Eurotunnel freight shuttle and severely damaged a section of the tunnel, injuring 34 people -- there had been a short-term impact on passenger numbers.

"We haven't made any alteration to our plans. We see this fire as an isolated case. But after the fire, passenger figures were down," Hornby told a a London news conference to mark British legislatative clearance to build a 2.8 billion pound rail link to run high-speed trains to the Channel Tunnel.

Hours after Eurostar's comments, Anglo-French Channel Tunnel operator Eurotunnel reported that another small fire had broken out on a platform at Folkestone in southern England at 0543 GMT but was soon snuffed out, with no casualties.

A spokeswoman for the trouble-prone tunnel told Reuters "There was a very small fire on the platform on the UK side of the tunnel. It was due to an electrical fault and lasted half an hour." No passengers were involved.

Eurostar, a joint venture between Eurostar UK and the French and Belgian national railways, is remaining silent about the level of compensation it expects to receive from Eurotunnel since the fire in November.
The group has been running about 90 percent of its trains since December 3, but no trains ran for 14 days after the fire.
Hornby said it was impossible to evaluate the total level of the company's claim against Eurotunnel -- as services were still not back to normal.
The rail link to the Channel Tunnel planned by the LCR consortium is one of the biggest civil engineering projects this century. Work is due to begin in 1998.

It will be capable of running high-speed trains to the Channel Tunnel at the port of Folkestone, south east England, with a maximum speed of 186 miles per hour and is expected to cut travel times to continental destinations by 35 minutes.
The construction will be funded partly by Eurostar flotation proceeds, with remaining money raised from bank finance and possibly revenues from the passenger service itself.
Eurostar says passenger numbers have picked up recently. Thursday's traffic -- at 10,000 passengers -- compared with pre-fire levels of around 12,000 passengers.
The LCR consortium includes coach company National Express Group, British entrepreneur Richard Branson's Virgin Group, SBC Warburg, London Electricity and engineering group Bechtel. ($1=.5982 Pound)
